## Digital progress—for whom?


```{=html}
<div class="photo-layout"><div class="photo-text"><p class="hero">We thought we knew which country would lead.</p><p>Then we changed the age group.</p><p class="quiet">Nokwanele Pretty Gwebu and Kay-Lee Dramat<br>Age and digital skills in Europe</p></div><div class="photo-image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," alt="Illustration labelled digital transformation, with a progress indicator and branching paths"></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
Kay-Lee: We started with an expectation about Estonia and its digital reputation. The results made us ask whose experience we mean when we describe a country as digitally advanced. Before the data, think of someone asking for help with their phone. The opening illustration is conceptual, not a data visual. Image supplied by the authors; original creator and source credit still need confirming. The supplied image is small, so avoid enlarging it further without a higher-resolution original.
:::

## “Where did the thing I copied go?”


```{=html}
<div class="photo-layout"><div class="photo-text"><p class="hero">You explain it.<br>They try again.</p><p>Perhaps you take the phone and do it.</p><p><strong>What happens when you aren’t there?</strong></p></div><div class="photo-image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," alt="A younger woman and an older woman looking at a tablet together"><p class="image-caption">Illustrative image supplied by the authors.</p></div></div>
```

::: {.notes}
Kay-Lee: Think of someone in your family asking how to take a screenshot, or where to find something they copied. Maybe you talk them through it. Maybe you do it because it feels quicker. Now imagine they need to do something important and you are not there. This photograph illustrates support between generations; we do not know the relationship of the people pictured. Eurostat does not measure these exact tasks or reliance on relatives here. Image supplied by the authors; original photographer/source credit still needs confirming.
:::
## We expected Estonia to stand out

::::::: {.chapter}
Our starting assumption
:::::::

::::::: {.expectation}
After reading about Estonia’s digital reputation, we thought we had a fairly good idea of what we would find.
:::::::

**Apparently, the data had other plans.**

::::::: {.quiet}
We compared reported digital activities across age groups, using Eurostat’s basic or above-basic digital-skills indicator.
:::::::

::::::: {.notes}
Pretty: This was our starting expectation, not a conclusion we had already proved. We thought Estonia would stand out. We chose to look at Germany and Romania too, with the EU as context. The measure is the share of people in each age group who meet Eurostat’s basic or above-basic digital-skills threshold. It comes from reported activities, not a practical test. Let’s start with younger adults.
:::::::

## Among younger adults, the result fitted our expectations

::::::: {.story-line}
At ages 25–34, Estonia’s estimate is about 86%, compared with about 70% in Germany. 2025.
:::::::

::::::: {.source}
Eurostat · isoc_sk_dskl_i21 · I_DSK2_BAB · percentage of individuals
:::::::

::::::: {.notes}
Pretty: At first, this looked fairly close to what we had expected. Estonia’s estimate for ages 25 to 34 was 86%, Germany’s about 70%. Each bar refers to the percentage in that age group, not in the whole country. We then asked whether this comparison held for older adults. The difference before rounding is 16.1 percentage points.
:::::::

## Then we looked at older adults

::::::: {.story-line}
At ages 65–74, Germany’s estimate is about 41%, compared with about 20% in Estonia. 2025.
:::::::

::::::: {.source}
Eurostat · isoc_sk_dskl_i21 · I_DSK2_BAB · percentage of individuals
:::::::

::::::: {.notes}
Pretty: Here the order reverses. Germany’s estimate is about 41%, Estonia’s about 20%. Same countries, same year, but a different answer when we change the age group. This is where our question changed. Instead of only asking which country leads, we started asking whose skills its reputation describes. Kay checked whether we had just found an unusual result in one year.
:::::::

::::::: {.notes}
Kay-Lee: We did not want to build the whole story on one year. We checked 2021 and 2023. Estonia stays above Germany in the younger group; Germany stays above Estonia in the older group. That makes the finding more persistent than a single snapshot. It still does not tell us why it happens. These are different surveys, not the same individuals followed over time, and we have not tested statistical significance. Source reliability flags and comparability notes still need reviewing.
:::::::


## Then we looked beyond our two-country comparison


```{=html}
<div class="circle-layout"><img src="images/europe_digital_skills_lifted.png" alt="Circular visual of 27 EU countries, each with six age bands in 2025"><div class="circle-copy"><p>27 countries.<br>Six age groups.<br>One question:</p><p><strong>Who shares in digital progress?</strong></p><p class="quiet">Youngest age group inside.<br>Oldest outside.<br>Colour shows percentages.</p></div></div>
```

::: {.source}
Eurostat · 2025 · Equal-sized segments do not represent population sizes.
:::

::: {.notes}
Kay-Lee: This is the visual that first made us stop and look more closely. Each country has six age bands, from 16–24 inside to 65–74 outside. Colour represents the share with basic or above-basic digital skills. Germany, Estonia and Romania are pulled outward. We were also struck by the Netherlands, Ireland, Denmark and Finland. We used this overview to explore patterns; the next chart makes the two age groups easier to compare precisely. Source: Eurostat isoc_sk_dskl_i21, I_DSK2_BAB, PC_IND. The circular chart shows 162 estimates, 27 countries times six age groups.
:::

We do not need to read every row aloud; the point is that the direction is consistent while the size varies.
:::::::

## The same age group tells very different national stories

::::::: {.story-line}
Among adults aged 65–74, estimates range from 7.3% in Romania to 69.6% in Ireland. 2025.
:::::::

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1120 430" role="img" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;height:auto"><text x="0" y="65" fill="#f8f3e9" font-size="29" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Ireland</text><rect x="190" y="35" width="696.3" height="44" fill="#ffd080"/><text x="901.3" y="68" fill="#ffd080" font-size="30" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">69.6%</text><text x="0" y="150" fill="#f8f3e9" font-size="29" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Germany</text><rect x="190" y="120" width="411.59999999999997" height="44" fill="#ffd080"/><text x="616.5999999999999" y="153" fill="#ffd080" font-size="30" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">41.2%</text><text x="0" y="235" fill="#f8f3e9" font-size="29" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Estonia</text><rect x="190" y="205" width="202.7" height="44" fill="#ffd080"/><text x="407.7" y="238" fill="#ffd080" font-size="30" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">20.3%</text><text x="0" y="320" fill="#f8f3e9" font-size="29" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Romania</text><rect x="190" y="290" width="72.6" height="44" fill="#ffd080"/><text x="277.6" y="323" fill="#ffd080" font-size="30" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" text-anchor="start">7.3%</text></svg>
```


::::::: {.source}
Eurostat · isoc_sk_dskl_i21 · I_DSK2_BAB · percentage of individuals
:::::::

::::::: {.notes}
Pretty: If age alone explained everything, these differences would be hard to account for. In Ireland, the estimate among adults aged 65 to 74 is close to 70%. In Romania, it is about 7%. Germany and Estonia fall between them. These results make us curious about the different contexts people live in. They cannot tell us which explanation is correct. We should also remember that people within each country have different experiences.
:::::::

## Back to the person asking for help

::::::: {.columns}
:::::: {.column width="57%"}
::::: {.hero}
This time, it’s an appointment they need to book.
:::::

The form is online.
::::::
:::::: {.column width="43%"}
The person who usually helps is unavailable.

**What would they need to complete it themselves?**

::::: {.quiet}
An imagined situation connecting the topic to everyday life. Eurostat does not measure reliance on family help here.
:::::
::::::

:::::::

::::::: {.notes}
Kay-Lee: Think back to the person asking about their phone. This time, imagine the task is booking an appointment. If someone usually helps, what happens when they are not there? We cannot use these data to claim how many people face that situation. But the findings give us a reason to take it seriously, and to ask what makes a service manageable for different people. We are not judging someone’s ability from their age. We are asking whether their experience gets considered.
:::::::


## There are places where someone can ask for help


```{=html}
<div class="photo-layout"><div class="photo-text"><p class="programme">Germany: Sparkasse Leipzig + VHS Nordsachsen</p><p>Free online-banking training for older adults.</p><p>Practical guidance, safe use and time for questions.</p><p class="quiet">Documented example: Oschatz, March 2026.</p></div><div class="photo-image"><img src="data:image/webp;base64," alt="A group of older adults gathered around a bank machine during an apparent demonstration"><p class="image-caption">Banking-help image supplied by the authors; the pictured event is unverified.</p></div></div>
```

::: {.source}
[Source: Sparkasse Leipzig, 12 March 2026](https://www.sparkasse-leipzig.de/de/home/ihre-sparkasse/pressecenter/details.html?news=v1m8271)
:::

::: {.notes}
Kay-Lee: We did not want to leave the story at the gap. There are practical examples of support. Sparkasse Leipzig and VHS Nordsachsen advertised a free course for older adults in Oschatz in March 2026. It covered online banking, the Sparkasse app and safe use, with time for questions. It was open to interested people, not only customers. This is one documented course, not a claim about all Sparkassen. The user-supplied photo appears to show an in-person banking demonstration, but we have not verified where or when. Do not identify it as the Leipzig course. Source, accessed 5 November 2026: https://www.sparkasse-leipzig.de/de/home/ihre-sparkasse/pressecenter/details.html?news=v1m8271. Image original source and photographer still need confirming.
:::

## Support also exists in Estonia and Romania

::: {.programme}
Estonia: Tallinn Libraries
:::

::: {.programme-detail}
Free individual and group digital guidance for seniors, including email, online purchases and payments.
:::

::: {.programme}
Romania: Hi Digital, Vodafone Foundation
:::

::: {.programme-detail}
Free practical workshops for adults aged 65+, covering smartphones, online payments and safety.
:::

::: {.source}
[Tallinn Libraries](https://tallinnaraamatukogud.ee/onnelik-ja-nutikas-seenior/) · [Vodafone Foundation Romania](https://fundatia-vodafone.ro/proiecte/hi-digital/)  
Examples of available support, not evidence that the national gaps have closed.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pretty: We found support in Estonia and Romania too. Tallinn Libraries offer free individual and group guidance for seniors, including help with payments and everyday digital difficulties. In Romania, Vodafone Foundation’s Hi Digital offers practical workshops and learning resources for people over 65. That matters to our story: a low national estimate does not mean that nobody is working on the problem. These programme descriptions show that help exists; they do not establish effectiveness or explain our Eurostat results. A brief mention of each is enough. Sources accessed 5 November 2026: https://tallinnaraamatukogud.ee/onnelik-ja-nutikas-seenior/ and https://fundatia-vodafone.ro/proiecte/hi-digital/
:::
## So, whose experience counts as digital progress?

::::::: {.chapter}
What changed our minds
:::::::

::::::: {.lead}
Estonia’s lead over Germany reversed when we changed the age group.

That reversal appeared in all three years.

Across Europe, older adults’ results also differed widely between countries.
:::::::

**The gaps are real. So are the places offering help.**

What would make that help easier to find for someone in your family?

::::::: {.notes}
Pretty: Our investigation started with an expectation about which country would lead. We found that the answer depends on the age group. Kay-Lee: We came back to the everyday question we started with. When you picture someone in your own family, what would being able to manage independently actually involve? The examples of support give us somewhere practical to end. They are not proof that the gaps have closed, but they show that help need not rest entirely with relatives. What would make that help easier for someone in your family to find?
:::::::

## Data and limits

Eurostat: **Individuals’ level of digital skills**  
`isoc_sk_dskl_i21` · `I_DSK2_BAB` · `PC_IND`

Reported activities, rather than a direct skills test.  
Group estimates; ages 75+ outside our selection.  
Descriptive comparisons without causal or significance claims.

[Data source](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/isoc_sk_dskl_i21/default/table?lang=en) · [Accompanying report](index.qmd)

::::::: {.notes}
Reference slide for questions. The extract contains 504 records: 27 countries plus the EU aggregate, six age groups, three years. Ireland ages 16–24 in 2021 is the only missing value and does not enter these charts. Source-quality flags and comparability checks remain outstanding. Each presenter has a substantive finding in the suggested allocation. Personal examples are invitations to reflect, not invented autobiographical experiences. Rehearse the notes and change any phrase that would feel unnatural for the person saying it.
:::::::
